focus: Chapter 2 names all the sons of Israel and then turns to Judah, tracing the line from Judah through Perez and Hezron to Jesse and David within the wider families of Hezron’s sons Jerahmeel and Caleb.

sections.title: The Sons of Israel
sections.summary: The twelve sons of Israel are named, from Reuben to Asher.

sections.title: The Sons of Judah
sections.summary: Judah’s sons are listed, including Er, who was wicked in the sight of the LORD, and Perez and Zerah, born to him by Tamar. The line of Zerah includes Achar, the troubler of Israel.

sections.title: The Line from Hezron to David
sections.summary: Hezron’s sons are named, and through Ram the line runs to Nahshon, Boaz, Obed, and Jesse. Jesse’s sons are listed with David the seventh, followed by their sisters Zeruiah and Abigail and their sons.

sections.title: The Family of Caleb the Son of Hezron
sections.summary: Caleb’s descendants include Hur, Uri, and Bezalel. Hezron’s later children and the towns of Jair are also recorded.

sections.title: The Family of Jerahmeel
sections.summary: Jerahmeel’s descendants are traced, including Sheshan, who had no sons and gave his daughter as wife to Jarha, his Egyptian servant, through whom the line continued.

sections.title: Further Descendants of Caleb
sections.summary: More of Caleb’s descendants are listed, many named as the fathers of towns in Judah, ending with the families of the scribes who dwelt at Jabez.

1.brief: The sons of Israel are named, beginning with Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun. Chronicles presents Israel as a family of twelve sons before focusing on any one tribe.
1.explain:
“These were the sons of Israel:”

Chapter 1 closed with the chiefs of Edom. Chapter 2 opens with the family whose story the whole book will tell. “The sons of Israel” are Jacob's twelve sons, the ancestors of Israel's tribes. Chronicles has already called Jacob by his God-given name, Israel (1:34), and the name now passes to the family that will become the nation. For readers after the exile, many of whose tribal connections had been shaken by deportation and loss, this line restated who they were: the descendants of the twelve sons of Israel.

“Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun,”

The first six names are the sons of Leah, listed in order of birth (Genesis 35:23). “Reuben” was the firstborn, though he lost the rights of the firstborn because of his sin against his father (1 Chronicles 5:1). “Levi” became the priestly tribe, whose service fills much of Chronicles. “Judah,” the fourth son, is the tribe whose genealogy will occupy the rest of this chapter and much of the next two, because from Judah came David. Even here, at the start, the whole family is named before attention narrows to Judah.
1.notes:
Chronicles keeps the birth order of Leah’s six sons from Genesis 35:23 but does not follow Genesis 35:24–26 in grouping the other six sons by their mothers.

Chapters 2–8 trace the tribes of Israel, with Judah first (2:3–4:23), Levi at the center (chapter 6), and Benjamin last (chapter 8).

The community after the exile centered on Judah and Benjamin together with priests and Levites, though some from Ephraim and Manasseh also lived in Jerusalem (9:3). The placement of Judah and Benjamin at the beginning and end may reflect that setting.

2.brief: The list of Israel’s sons concludes with Dan, Joseph, Benjamin, Naphtali, Gad, and Asher. Naming all twelve keeps the whole people in view, even though Judah will receive the most attention.
2.explain:
“Dan, Joseph, Benjamin, Naphtali, Gad, and Asher.”

The remaining six sons are named. “Joseph” and “Benjamin” were the sons of Rachel, Jacob's beloved wife. “Dan” and “Naphtali” were born to Bilhah, Rachel's servant, and “Gad” and “Asher” to Zilpah, Leah's servant (Genesis 35:24–26). By naming all twelve, Chronicles keeps the whole people of Israel in view. Judah will receive the most attention, but it never stands alone. The book's later concern with “all Israel” begins here, with twelve brothers named together as one family.
2.notes:
Dan is placed before Joseph and Benjamin rather than with his full brother Naphtali. The reason for the arrangement is not stated.

Some suggest that Dan, Rachel’s son through her maid Bilhah (Genesis 30:3–6), is placed with Rachel’s own sons because Rachel counted him as her own; others connect his position with his seventh place in Jacob’s blessing (Genesis 49:16).

Joseph is named as one son, though his descendants became two tribes, Ephraim and Manasseh (Genesis 48:5). Chronicles later explains that the birthright passed to Joseph's sons while leadership came through Judah (1 Chronicles 5:1–2).

3.brief: Judah’s first three sons, Er, Onan, and Shelah, were born to him by the daughter of Shua the Canaanitess. Er, the firstborn, was wicked in the sight of the LORD, so the LORD put him to death, showing that belonging to Judah did not place anyone beyond God’s judgment.
3.explain:
“The sons of Judah were Er, Onan, and Shelah.”

The genealogy now turns to Judah, the tribe of David. Judah's first three sons are named. Their story is told in Genesis 38.

“These three were born to him by the daughter of Shua, the Canaanitess.”

Their mother was “the daughter of Shua,” a Canaanite woman (Genesis 38:2). Chronicles notes her Canaanite background without comment. The royal tribe of Judah included Canaanite ancestry from its earliest generation, a reminder that Israel's family history was never as tidy or isolated as later pride might wish.

“Er, the firstborn of Judah, was wicked in the sight of the LORD; so He killed him.”

The verse adds a sobering note. “Er, the firstborn” was “wicked in the sight of the LORD,” and the LORD put him to death (Genesis 38:7). Scripture does not say what Er's wickedness was. What matters is the verdict: the LORD saw it, judged it, and acted. The first notice of moral evaluation in the tribal genealogies concerns a son of Judah, the royal tribe. Belonging to Judah did not place anyone beyond God's judgment. The genealogy that leads toward David begins by reminding the reader that God is holy and that privilege does not excuse sin.
3.notes:
“The daughter of Shua” renders the Hebrew bat-shua', which can also be read as a personal name, Bathshua. The same form is used for Bathsheba in 1 Chronicles 3:5. Genesis 38:2 indicates that Shua was the name of her father.

Chronicles does not mention that Onan was also put to death by the LORD (Genesis 38:8–10). It records only Er's judgment, perhaps because Er was the firstborn.

Shelah's descendants are listed later, in 4:21–23, and became the clan of the Shelanites (Numbers 26:20).

4.brief: Tamar, Judah’s daughter-in-law, bore him Perez and Zerah, bringing Judah’s sons to five. The brief note recalls the troubled events of Genesis 38 through which the family continued, without approving them.
4.explain:
“And Tamar, his daughter-in-law, bore him Perez and Zerah.”

The line continues through one of the most uncomfortable episodes in Genesis. “Tamar” was the widow of Judah's son Er. When Judah failed to give her his son Shelah as he had promised, she disguised herself and conceived twins by Judah himself (Genesis 38:11–30). Chronicles compresses that story into a single phrase: “his daughter-in-law.” The words are enough to recall what happened. Chronicles does not hide the circumstances and does not approve them. It simply states that “Perez and Zerah” were born to Judah through Tamar.

The line through Perez will lead to David (2:5, 9–15). Ruth 4 also traces David's ancestry through Perez and remembers Tamar by name (Ruth 4:12, 18). Matthew names her in the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:3). God worked His purposes through a family whose history included deception and failure, and the genealogies do not pretend otherwise.

“All the sons of Judah were five.”

The verse totals Judah's sons: Er, Onan, Shelah, Perez, and Zerah. The count includes the two who died, so all five are remembered.
4.notes: Judah himself acknowledged of Tamar, “She has been more righteous than I” (Genesis 38:26).

5.brief: Perez’s sons are Hezron and Hamul. Through Hezron the line that leads to David will be traced.
5.explain:
“The sons of Perez were Hezron and Hamul.”

The list follows “Perez,” the elder twin, into the next generation. His two sons, “Hezron” and “Hamul,” are named in the list of those who went down to Egypt with Jacob (Genesis 46:12) and as heads of clans in Numbers 26:21. Through “Hezron” the line that leads to David will be traced. Hezron's three sons will organize most of the rest of this chapter (2:9). Hamul's descendants are not traced further in Chronicles.

6.brief: Zerah’s five sons are listed: Zimri, Ethan, Heman, Calcol, and Dara. The record follows Judah’s other line through Tamar before returning to Perez.
6.explain:
“The sons of Zerah were Zimri, Ethan, Heman, Calcol, and Dara—five of them in all.”

Before following Perez's line, the record lists the family of “Zerah,” Perez's twin. His five sons are named. “Zimri” is probably the same man called Zabdi in Joshua 7:1, the grandfather of Achan. “Ethan, Heman, Calcol,” and “Dara” have names that appear in 1 Kings 4:31, where Solomon's wisdom is said to surpass that of “Ethan the Ezrahite, and Heman, Chalcol, and Darda.” Psalm 88 is attributed to Heman the Ezrahite and Psalm 89 to Ethan the Ezrahite. “Ezrahite” may mean ‘descendant of Zerah.’ If these are the same men, Zerah's family was remembered for wisdom. The record follows Judah's other line through Tamar before returning to Perez.
6.notes:
“Dara” corresponds to “Darda” in 1 Kings 4:31. Some Hebrew and Greek manuscripts, along with the ancient Syriac translation and the Latin Vulgate translation, read “Darda” in this verse as well, and some translations (for example, the NIV and NLT) adopt that form. The standard Hebrew text reads Dara.

1 Kings 4:31 describes the wise men it names as “the sons of Mahol.” Mahol may be a personal name. Because the same Hebrew word (machol) means ‘dance’ (Psalm 30:11), some have taken the phrase to mean members of a guild of musicians or dancers rather than literal sons, though few interpreters have adopted this view.

Heman and Ethan are also names of Levitical singers in David's time (1 Chronicles 6:33, 44; 15:19). The relationship among these figures is uncertain.

Zimri is a different man from Zimri the Simeonite (Numbers 25:14) and Zimri the king of Israel (1 Kings 16:9–20).

7.brief: Carmi’s son Achar is remembered as the troubler of Israel, who transgressed in the accursed thing. He is the Achan of Joshua 7, and the form of his name here fits his description, showing that the family record also preserves accountability for unfaithfulness.
7.explain:
“The son of Carmi was Achar,”

The genealogy moves to a notorious member of Zerah's family. “Carmi” was apparently the son of Zimri (Joshua 7:1 traces Achan's descent from Zerah through Zabdi and Carmi). His son was “Achar.” Joshua calls him Achan. Chronicles uses the form “Achar,” which sounds like the Hebrew word for ‘trouble.’

“the troubler of Israel,”

His name fits his description. Achar is remembered as “the troubler of Israel.” At Jericho he took for himself silver, gold, and a garment that God had devoted to destruction, and Israel was defeated at Ai because of his sin (Joshua 7:1–26). Joshua said to him, “Why have you troubled us? The LORD will trouble you this day” (Joshua 7:25). The place of his execution was called the Valley of Achor, ‘valley of trouble.’

“who transgressed in the accursed thing.”

Chronicles states the nature of his sin. “Transgressed” describes unfaithfulness, a breach of trust against God. “The accursed thing” refers to the spoil of Jericho that God had devoted to Himself and forbidden Israel to take (Joshua 6:17–19). Achar's sin brought trouble on the whole nation. The family record of Judah preserves his name as a warning. A genealogy that leads to David does not omit those whose unfaithfulness harmed God's people.
7.notes:
In Hebrew, the name Achar ('akar) and the word translated “troubler” ('oker) come from the same word family. The name Achor, used for the valley in Joshua 7:26, belongs to that word family as well. Some translations of Chronicles read “Achan” here, as in Joshua.

“Transgressed” translates the Hebrew verb ma'al, a key word in Chronicles for unfaithfulness toward God. The same verb describes the unfaithfulness behind the exile of the northern tribes (5:25) and Saul’s death (10:13), and the related noun describes the unfaithfulness for which Judah was exiled (9:1). Its first appearance in the book is in connection with Achar.

8.brief: Ethan’s son is Azariah. This brief note completes the record of Zerah’s descendants.
8.explain:
“The son of Ethan was Azariah.”

This brief note completes the record of Zerah's descendants. “Ethan,” one of Zerah's sons (2:6), had a son named “Azariah.” Nothing more is known of him. Azariah was a common name in Israel, meaning ‘the LORD has helped.’ With this note, the record of Zerah's family closes, and the genealogy returns to Perez's son Hezron, whose line leads to David. Even a single name like Azariah's is preserved; the record remembers people about whom Scripture tells us nothing else.
8.notes: The Old Testament mentions more than twenty men named Azariah, and roughly seventeen of them appear in Chronicles. This Azariah, a descendant of Zerah, is different from the priests, kings, and others who bore the same name.

9.brief: Hezron’s sons are named: Jerahmeel, Ram, and Chelubai. These three sons organize much of the chapter, and Chelubai is the Caleb of verse 18.
9.explain:
“Also the sons of Hezron who were born to him were Jerahmeel, Ram, and Chelubai.”

The genealogy now reaches the three sons of “Hezron” who organize most of the rest of the chapter. “Jerahmeel” was the firstborn (2:25). His descendants, the Jerahmeelites, lived in the southern part of Judah (1 Samuel 27:10). “Ram” is the son through whom the line leads to David (2:10–17). “Chelubai” is another form of the name Caleb, as verse 18 shows. The chapter will trace all three lines: Ram's line to David (2:10–17), Caleb's family (2:18–24, 42–55), and Jerahmeel's family (2:25–41). David's ancestry is placed within the wider family of Judah, among brothers and cousins who also had their place in the tribe.
9.notes:
Ram is named second among Hezron’s sons but is treated first in the detailed listing, ahead of Jerahmeel the firstborn.

A related form of the name, “Chelub,” appears in 4:11.

10.brief: Ram fathered Amminadab, and Amminadab fathered Nahshon, leader of the children of Judah. The line toward David passes through a recognized tribal leader of the wilderness generation (Numbers 1:7; 2:3).
10.explain:
“Ram begot Amminadab, and Amminadab begot Nahshon,”

The line toward David begins with “Ram,” Hezron's son. Ram fathered “Amminadab,” and Amminadab fathered “Nahshon.” Amminadab was the father-in-law of Aaron, since Aaron married “Elisheba, daughter of Amminadab, sister of Nahshon” (Exodus 6:23). The family of Judah's future kings was linked by marriage to the family of Israel's first high priest.

“leader of the children of Judah;”

Nahshon is given a title: “leader of the children of Judah.” In the wilderness, Nahshon led the tribe of Judah. He is named among the tribal leaders who assisted Moses with the census (Numbers 1:7), and he led Judah's camp when Israel marched (Numbers 2:3). He brought the first offering at the dedication of the tabernacle altar (Numbers 7:12). The line toward David passed through a recognized leader of the wilderness generation.
10.notes:
From Nahshon to David the line has only four more names (Salma, Boaz, Obed, Jesse), spanning the period from the wilderness to the early monarchy.

Some interpreters suggest the list may be selective, though Ruth 4:20–22 gives the same sequence. The genealogy does not supply ages, so its chronological span cannot be calculated from the names alone.

11.brief: Nahshon fathered Salma, and Salma fathered Boaz. The line now reaches Boaz, whose story in the book of Ruth stands behind this brief entry.
11.explain:
“Nahshon begot Salma, and Salma begot Boaz;”

The line continues. “Salma” was Nahshon's son, and “Boaz” was Salma's son. Boaz was the Bethlehem landowner who acted as Ruth's kinsman-redeemer. As a close relative of her late husband, he bought the family property and married Ruth the Moabitess, preserving her late husband's family line (Ruth 4:9–13). Matthew adds that Salmon (Salma) fathered Boaz “by Rahab” (Matthew 1:5), the woman of Jericho who sheltered Israel's spies. Chronicles mentions neither Rahab nor Ruth. It names the men in the line, and the reader who knows the book of Ruth fills in the story behind the name “Boaz.”
11.notes:
Ruth 4:20–21 and Matthew 1:4–5 read “Salmon.” Chronicles reads “Salma” here and in 2:51. The forms are variants.

The Salma of 2:51, “the father of Bethlehem,” is listed among Caleb's descendants through Hur. Whether he is the same man as Salma the father of Boaz is uncertain, though the connection with Bethlehem is suggestive.

12.brief: Boaz fathered Obed, and Obed fathered Jesse. The genealogy closely matches Ruth 4:21–22 and brings the line to David’s father.
12.explain:
“Boaz begot Obed, and Obed begot Jesse;”

The line reaches David's father. “Obed” was the son born to Boaz and Ruth, whom the women of Bethlehem celebrated as a restorer of life to Naomi (Ruth 4:13–17). Obed's son was “Jesse” of Bethlehem. This sequence closely matches the genealogy at the end of Ruth: “Boaz begot Obed; Obed begot Jesse, and Jesse begot David” (Ruth 4:21–22). With Jesse, the line has nearly reached its goal. The next verses will name Jesse's sons, building toward David.
12.notes: This Obed, David's grandfather, is a different person from Obed the descendant of Jerahmeel (2:37–38).

13.brief: Jesse’s sons are listed in order of birth, beginning with Eliab his firstborn, Abinadab the second, and Shimea the third. The careful numbering builds toward the youngest son.
13.explain:
“Jesse begot Eliab his firstborn, Abinadab the second, Shimea the third,”

Jesse's sons are now listed in order of birth, each with his number. “Eliab his firstborn” was tall and impressive; when Samuel saw him, he thought, “Surely the LORD's anointed is before Him!” But the LORD answered that He looks at the heart (1 Samuel 16:6–7). “Abinadab the second” and “Shimea the third” also passed before Samuel and were not chosen (1 Samuel 16:8–9). The three oldest later served in Saul's army when Goliath challenged Israel (1 Samuel 17:13). The careful numbering builds toward the youngest son.
13.notes:
“Shimea” is called “Shammah” in 1 Samuel 16:9 and 17:13 and “Shimeah” in 2 Samuel 13:3, where his son Jonadab appears. These are variant forms of the same name.

This Abinadab, David's brother, is one of three men by that name in 1 Samuel: the man in whose house the ark rested (1 Samuel 7:1), David's brother, and Saul's son (1 Samuel 31:2).

14.brief: Nethanel the fourth and Raddai the fifth continue the count of Jesse’s sons. The steady sequence keeps the reader moving toward David.
14.explain:
“Nethanel the fourth, Raddai the fifth,”

The count of Jesse's sons continues. “Nethanel the fourth” and “Raddai the fifth” are not named in the narratives of 1 Samuel, which mention only the three oldest brothers by name. Chronicles preserves their names. The steady sequence of numbers keeps the reader moving toward David. Each brother has his place in the family, even though the story of God's choice will focus on the youngest.

15.brief: Ozem is the sixth son, and David is named the seventh. Here David is counted seventh, while 1 Samuel 16:10–11 and 17:12 indicate eight sons of Jesse, a difference this chapter does not explain.
15.explain:
“Ozem the sixth,”

“Ozem” is the sixth son. Like Nethanel and Raddai, he is otherwise unknown.

“and David the seventh.”

The list reaches its goal with “David the seventh.” David, the shepherd chosen by God, anointed by Samuel, and made king over all Israel, is the reason this line has been traced. Chronicles will devote most of the remainder of the book to his reign (chapters 10–29). Here, in the genealogy, he is simply the youngest son of Jesse, numbered after his brothers. God's choice of the youngest son echoes His pattern of choosing those whom people overlook (1 Samuel 16:11–13).

1 Samuel indicates that Jesse had eight sons. Seven passed before Samuel, and David was the eighth (1 Samuel 16:10–11; 17:12). Chronicles counts David as the seventh. The chapter does not explain the difference.
15.notes:
Several explanations have been proposed for the difference between this verse and 1 Samuel 16:10–11 and 17:12. One brother may have died young or without children and so was omitted from the genealogy.

1 Chronicles 27:18 names “Elihu, one of David’s brothers,” who is not listed here, though Elihu may be another form of Eliab, and the ancient Greek translation known as the Septuagint reads Eliab in that verse.

An ancient translation of this verse into the Syriac language adds Elihu as the seventh son and counts David as the eighth.

16.brief: Jesse’s daughters Zeruiah and Abigail are named, together with Zeruiah’s three sons, Abishai, Joab, and Asahel. These nephews of David are men who appear as leading warriors in his later reign.
16.explain:
“Now their sisters were Zeruiah and Abigail.”

The genealogy names Jesse's daughters, an unusual inclusion. “Zeruiah” and “Abigail” were David's sisters. Their names matter because of the sons they bore, who played major roles in David's reign.

“And the sons of Zeruiah were Abishai, Joab, and Asahel—three.”

Zeruiah's three sons were among David's most important military men. “Joab” became commander of David's army, fierce, capable, and often ruthless (1 Chronicles 11:6; 18:15). “Abishai” was a leading warrior and commander (1 Chronicles 11:20; 18:12). “Asahel” was famous for his speed, “as fleet of foot as a wild gazelle” (2 Samuel 2:18), and was killed by Abner. David's own nephews were among the men who helped establish his kingdom. Chronicles identifies them as part of Judah's family record.
16.notes:
2 Samuel 17:25 describes Abigail as “the daughter of Nahash, sister of Zeruiah.” This raises a question about whether Zeruiah and Abigail were Jesse's daughters or David's half-sisters through their mother's earlier marriage to a man named Nahash.

Some propose that Nahash was a former husband of Jesse's wife; others suggest Nahash was another name for Jesse or was the name of the mother. Chronicles calls them the sisters of Jesse's sons. The text does not supply enough information to resolve the relationship.

Joab, Abishai, and Asahel are regularly identified as “the sons of Zeruiah” rather than by their father's name (2 Samuel 2:18; 1 Chronicles 11:6), which is unusual and may indicate their mother's prominence as David's sister.

17.brief: Abigail bore Amasa, whose father was Jether the Ishmaelite. The record includes an Ishmaelite within the immediate family of David’s sister without further comment.
17.explain:
“Abigail bore Amasa;”

David's other sister, “Abigail,” had a son named “Amasa.” Amasa later commanded Absalom's army in the rebellion against David (2 Samuel 17:25). After the rebellion, David appointed him commander in Joab's place, and Joab murdered him (2 Samuel 19:13; 20:9–10). His story shows how deeply David's family was divided.

“and the father of Amasa was Jether the Ishmaelite.”

Amasa's father was “Jether the Ishmaelite.” The list includes an Ishmaelite within the immediate family of David's sister without comment. Along with the Canaanite mother of Judah's first three sons (2:3) and Ruth's Moabite ancestry behind the line of Boaz, Jether's presence shows that David's family history included people from outside Israel.
17.notes:
2 Samuel 17:25 calls Amasa's father “Jithra, an Israelite.” Jithra is a variant form of Jether.

The difference between “Ishmaelite” here and “Israelite” in 2 Samuel 17:25 may have arisen in copying, since the two Hebrew words (yishme'eli and yisre'eli) are similar in spelling. Others suggest that “Israelite” in 2 Samuel was itself significant, marking a man from the northern tribes who married into a family of Judah.

Some Greek manuscripts of 2 Samuel 17:25 read “Ishmaelite,” and several modern translations (for example, the ESV and NLT) adopt that reading there, since there would be little reason to note that an Israelite was an Israelite. Others, such as the NASB and NIV, keep “Israelite.” The question is unresolved.

18.brief: Caleb the son of Hezron has children by Azubah his wife and by Jerioth, and Jesher, Shobab, and Ardon are named. This Caleb is Hezron’s son and should be kept distinct from Caleb the son of Jephunneh (4:15).
18.explain:
“Caleb the son of Hezron”

The genealogy turns to Hezron's third son, called Chelubai in verse 9. “Caleb the son of Hezron” should be kept distinct from the better-known Caleb the son of Jephunneh, the faithful spy who followed the LORD fully (Numbers 13:6; 14:24). Chronicles lists Caleb the son of Jephunneh's family separately (4:15). This Caleb is identified by his descent from Hezron; the genealogy does not provide the ages needed to calculate the interval between the two Calebs.

“had children by Azubah, his wife, and by Jerioth.”

Caleb's children came from “Azubah, his wife,” and “Jerioth.” The Hebrew is difficult, and it is unclear whether Jerioth was a second wife or a daughter of Azubah.

“Now these were her sons: Jesher, Shobab, and Ardon.”

Three sons are named, apparently Azubah's sons. They are otherwise unknown. The record remembers the beginning of Caleb's family before turning to his son Hur.
18.notes:
The Hebrew reads literally ‘Caleb son of Hezron begot Azubah, a woman, and Jerioth.’ This could mean that Caleb fathered a daughter named Azubah or that he had children through Azubah and Jerioth. The NKJV and most translations take Azubah as his wife.

Whether “her sons” refers to Azubah or Jerioth is also unclear. Translations differ, and no explanation is certain.

Caleb the son of Jephunneh is called a Kenizzite (Numbers 32:12; Joshua 14:6), which suggests a family with non-Israelite roots incorporated into Judah. The relationship between the two Calebs' clans is uncertain.

19.brief: After Azubah dies, Caleb marries Ephrath, who bears him Hur. Through Hur, Caleb’s line will lead to Bezalel, the craftsman who helped build the tabernacle.
19.explain:
“When Azubah died, Caleb took Ephrath as his wife,”

After Azubah's death, Caleb married “Ephrath.” Her name is related to Ephrathah, an old name associated with Bethlehem (Ruth 4:11; Micah 5:2). The connection anticipates verses 50–51, where Ephrathah's son Hur is linked with Bethlehem.

“who bore him Hur.”

Ephrath bore Caleb a son, “Hur.” Through Hur, Caleb's line will lead to Bezalel, the tabernacle craftsman named in verse 20 and to the founders of several towns in Judah, including Bethlehem (2:50–51).
19.notes: Some interpreters identify this Hur with the Hur who, with Aaron, held up Moses's hands during the battle with Amalek (Exodus 17:12). That identification is possible, especially since Hur's grandson Bezalel belonged to the exodus generation (Exodus 31:2), but the text does not state it.

20.brief: Hur fathered Uri, and Uri fathered Bezalel. Bezalel is the craftsman whom God filled with His Spirit to build the tabernacle (Exodus 31:1–5), linking Judah’s families with the work of worship.
20.explain:
“And Hur begot Uri, and Uri begot Bezalel.”

The line from Caleb through Hur leads to “Bezalel,” one of the most honored craftsmen in Israel's history. When God gave Moses instructions for the tabernacle, He said, “See, I have called by name Bezalel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah. And I have filled him with the Spirit of God, in wisdom, in understanding, in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship” (Exodus 31:2–3). Bezalel built the ark, the tabernacle furnishings, and the bronze altar. Chronicles later notes that Solomon and the assembly sought the LORD at “the bronze altar that Bezalel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, had made” (2 Chronicles 1:5).

The notice links Judah's families with the work of worship. The tribe of Judah gave Israel its kings, and it also gave Israel the Spirit-filled craftsman who built the place where God met His people.

21.brief: Later, when he was sixty years old, Hezron married the daughter of Machir the father of Gilead, and she bore him Segub. The record connects Judah’s family with the clan of Machir in Gilead, east of the Jordan.
21.explain:
“Now afterward Hezron went in to the daughter of Machir the father of Gilead,”

The genealogy returns to “Hezron” and adds a later marriage. “Machir” was the son of Manasseh, and his descendants settled in Gilead, east of the Jordan (Numbers 32:39–40). “The father of Gilead” identifies Machir as the ancestor of the Gileadites. Hezron, of the tribe of Judah, married a woman from the tribe of Manasseh.

“whom he married when he was sixty years old;”

Chronicles notes Hezron's age, “sixty years old,” an unusual detail in a genealogy. The marriage came late in his life.

“and she bore him Segub.”

The son of this marriage was “Segub.” Through him, Judah's family was connected with the clan of Machir in Gilead, east of the Jordan. The tribes were not sealed off from one another; families intermarried, and their histories became intertwined.
21.notes:
This marriage explains why Segub’s son Jair (2:22) is called “Jair the son of Manasseh” in Numbers 32:41 and Deuteronomy 3:14, though his father’s line was from Judah.

Hezron went down to Egypt with Jacob (Genesis 46:12), while Jair belonged to the conquest generation. If the relationships are direct, a long period separates them; the genealogy may compress the generations. The text does not settle the question.

22.brief: Segub fathered Jair, who had twenty-three cities in the land of Gilead. The family’s influence extended into territory beyond the Jordan.
22.explain:
“Segub begot Jair,”

Segub's son was “Jair.” Jair is remembered in the books of Moses as a leader who captured towns in Gilead and Bashan and named them after himself, Havoth Jair, ‘the tent villages of Jair’ (Numbers 32:41; Deuteronomy 3:14).

“who had twenty-three cities in the land of Gilead.”

Jair possessed “twenty-three cities” in Gilead. The family's influence extended into the territory east of the Jordan. Jair traced his father's line to Judah and was connected to Manasseh through his paternal grandmother. He became a significant landholder among the eastern tribes.
22.notes: Judges 10:4 mentions thirty towns called Havoth Jair belonging to Jair the Gileadite, a judge, who may be a later descendant. Deuteronomy 3:4 and Joshua 13:30 refer to sixty cities in the region. The different figures likely reflect different periods or different groupings of the towns. Chronicles' figure of twenty-three applies to Jair's possession in Gilead.

23.brief: A parenthesis notes that Geshur and Syria took from them the towns of Jair, with Kenath and its towns, sixty towns in all, and that all these belonged to the sons of Machir. The record honestly preserves the loss of territory as well as its earlier possession.
23.explain:
“(Geshur and Syria took from them the towns of Jair,”

A parenthesis adds a note of loss. “Geshur” was a small Aramean kingdom northeast of the Sea of Galilee. “Syria” translates the Hebrew name Aram, referring here to the Aramean peoples to the north. At some point these neighbors captured “the towns of Jair.” The family that had once held these towns lost them.

“with Kenath and its towns—sixty towns.)”

Along with Jair's towns, the Arameans took “Kenath and its towns,” a total of “sixty towns.” Kenath was taken by Nobah during the conquest (Numbers 32:42). The list honestly preserves the loss of territory as well as its earlier possession. Chronicles does not pretend that Israel's history was a story of uninterrupted success.

“All these belonged to the sons of Machir the father of Gilead.”

The verse closes by identifying the whole region with “the sons of Machir.” The towns of Jair and Kenath belonged to Machir's descendants, the clan into which Hezron had married. The note ties Hezron's family in Judah to the history of Manasseh's territory east of the Jordan.
23.notes:
The text does not say when Geshur and Aram captured these towns. It may refer to the period of the judges or to the later Aramean wars, when Hazael conquered Israel’s territory east of the Jordan, “including Gilead and Bashan” (2 Kings 10:32–33). David married Maacah, the daughter of the king of Geshur, and their son Absalom later fled to Geshur (1 Chronicles 3:2; 2 Samuel 13:37–38).

Here the sixty towns include Kenath and its towns together with the towns of Jair, while Joshua 13:30 applies the figure sixty to “all the towns of Jair which are in Bashan.”

24.brief: After Hezron dies in Caleb Ephrathah, his wife Abijah bears him Ashhur the father of Tekoa. A son born after his father’s death still receives his place in the family record.
24.explain:
“After Hezron died in Caleb Ephrathah,”

The record notes Hezron's death. “Caleb Ephrathah” appears to be a place name, perhaps a town or district associated with Caleb and his wife Ephrathah (2:19). The location is unknown.

“Hezron's wife Abijah bore him Ashhur the father of Tekoa.”

After his death, Hezron's wife “Abijah” gave birth to his son “Ashhur.” A son born after his father's death still received his place in the family record. Ashhur is called “the father of Tekoa,” meaning the ancestor or founder of the people of Tekoa, a town in the hill country south of Bethlehem. Tekoa was later the home of a wise woman sent to David (2 Samuel 14:2) and of the prophet Amos (Amos 1:1). Ashhur's family is listed in 4:5–7.
24.notes:
The NKJV identifies Abijah as Hezron’s wife. The phrase “in Caleb Ephrathah” does not by itself identify Ephrathah with Abijah or indicate another marriage.

“The father of Tekoa” is one of many expressions of this kind in this chapter (compare 2:21, 42–55) and in chapter 4 (for example, 4:4–5).

25.brief: The sons of Jerahmeel, Hezron’s firstborn, are listed: Ram the firstborn, Bunah, Oren, Ozem, and Ahijah. This Ram is Jerahmeel’s son, distinct from Jerahmeel’s brother Ram in verse 10.
25.explain:
“The sons of Jerahmeel, the firstborn of Hezron, were”

The genealogy now turns to Hezron's firstborn, “Jerahmeel.” His family occupies verses 25–41. The Jerahmeelites lived in the Negev, the southern region of Judah (1 Samuel 27:10; 30:29).

“Ram, the firstborn, and Bunah, Oren, Ozem, and Ahijah.”

Five sons are named. “Ram, the firstborn” is Jerahmeel's son, distinct from Jerahmeel's brother Ram, the ancestor of David (2:9–10). “Ozem” shares a name with David's brother (2:15). Names often recurred within the same tribe.
25.notes:
The last name, “Ahijah,” may identify a fifth son or a wife (‘from Ahijah’). The next verse's reference to “another wife” supports the second possibility. The ancient Greek translation known as the Septuagint instead reads ‘his brother.’ The NKJV treats Ahijah as a son.

In 1 Samuel 27:10 “the southern area of the Jerahmeelites” is named alongside “the southern area of Judah” and “the southern area of the Kenites” as a distinct region.

26.brief: Jerahmeel had another wife named Atarah, who was the mother of Onam. Through Onam the record will trace a further branch of the family.
26.explain:
“Jerahmeel had another wife, whose name was Atarah;”

Jerahmeel had a second wife, “Atarah.” Her name is preserved, which is unusual. The genealogy pauses to remember a wife and mother.

“she was the mother of Onam.”

Atarah's son was “Onam.” Through Onam, the record will trace a further branch of Jerahmeel's family (2:28–33). The family of Hezron's firstborn branched through more than one wife, and the record honors both lines.

27.brief: The sons of Ram, Jerahmeel’s firstborn, are Maaz, Jamin, and Eker. The first branch of Jerahmeel’s family is recorded briefly.
27.explain:
“The sons of Ram, the firstborn of Jerahmeel, were Maaz, Jamin, and Eker.”

The first branch of Jerahmeel's family is recorded briefly. “Ram” was Jerahmeel's firstborn (2:25), and his three sons were “Maaz, Jamin,” and “Eker.” None of them is mentioned elsewhere. Chronicles names them and moves on. Even branches of the family about which nothing else is known are preserved in the record of Judah.

28.brief: Onam’s sons are Shammai and Jada, and Shammai’s sons are Nadab and Abishur. The record follows Onam’s line through two generations.
28.explain:
“The sons of Onam were Shammai and Jada.”

The list follows “Onam,” Atarah's son (2:26). His two sons were “Shammai” and “Jada.” Both lines will be traced: Shammai's in verses 28–31 and Jada's in verses 32–33.

“The sons of Shammai were Nadab and Abishur.”

Shammai had two sons, “Nadab” and “Abishur.” The record follows Onam's line through two generations. These men are not otherwise identified in Scripture.
28.notes: This Nadab is unrelated to Nadab the son of Aaron (Exodus 6:23) and Nadab the king of Israel (1 Kings 15:25). This Shammai is different from Shammai the son of Rekem (2:44).

29.brief: Abishur’s wife is named as Abihail, and she bore him Ahban and Molid. The genealogy pauses to remember a wife and mother by name.
29.explain:
“And the name of the wife of Abishur was Abihail,”

The genealogy pauses again to name a wife. “Abihail” was the wife of “Abishur.” Her name means ‘my father is strength’ and was borne by both men and women in Israel.

“and she bore him Ahban and Molid.”

Abihail's two sons were “Ahban” and “Molid.” The genealogy names their mother before their names, giving her a place in the family history. Chronicles' genealogies regularly remember women in this way (2:16–17, 26, 34–35, 46, 48–49).

30.brief: Nadab’s sons are Seled and Appaim, and Seled died without children. The record notes that his line ended without passing judgment on the man himself.
30.explain:
“The sons of Nadab were Seled and Appaim;”

Chronicles follows Abishur's brother “Nadab” (2:28). His two sons were “Seled” and “Appaim.”

“Seled died without children.”

The list notes that “Seled died without children.” In Israel, dying without children meant that a man's name and inheritance would not continue, a grief that the law concerning marriage to a deceased brother's widow sought to prevent (Deuteronomy 25:5–6). Chronicles records the fact without passing judgment on Seled. His line ended, but his name is still remembered. The genealogy then continues through his brother Appaim.

31.brief: Appaim’s son is Ishi, Ishi’s son is Sheshan, and Sheshan’s son is Ahlai. The NKJV calls Ahlai Sheshan’s son, yet verse 34 says Sheshan had no sons, only daughters. The account does not explicitly explain how these statements fit together.
31.explain:
“The son of Appaim was Ishi, the son of Ishi was Sheshan,”

The line continues from “Appaim” through “Ishi” to “Sheshan.” Sheshan becomes important in verses 34–35, where his family's continuation is described.

“and Sheshan's son was Ahlai.”

The NKJV calls “Ahlai” Sheshan's son. Yet verse 34 says that “Sheshan had no sons, only daughters.” The genealogy does not explain how these statements fit together. Several possibilities have been suggested. Ahlai may have been a daughter, since the Hebrew word for “son” can sometimes mean ‘child’ in a broad sense, and some names were used by both men and women. Ahlai may have been a son who died before his father, leaving Sheshan without a son to continue the line. Or Ahlai may have been a grandson through Sheshan's daughter. The account itself does not resolve the question.
31.notes:
In Hebrew, each clause uses the plural expression ‘sons of’ before a single name. The last clause reads literally ‘the sons of Sheshan, Ahlai.’ The wording therefore does not show whether Ahlai was male or female.

A man named “Zabad the son of Ahlai” appears among David's mighty men (1 Chronicles 11:41). A Zabad also appears in Sheshan's line through his daughter (2:36).

Whether these are the same man is uncertain. The genealogy supplies no dates that establish or exclude the identification.

32.brief: The sons of Jada, Shammai’s brother, are Jether and Jonathan, and Jether died without children. Like Seled, Jether is still remembered by name though his line did not continue.
32.explain:
“The sons of Jada, the brother of Shammai, were Jether and Jonathan;”

The record now traces the second branch of Onam's family. “Jada” was Shammai's brother (2:28). His two sons were “Jether” and “Jonathan.”

“Jether died without children.”

Like Seled (2:30), “Jether died without children.” His line did not continue, but he is still remembered by name. The genealogy is willing to record the ends of family lines as well as their continuation. It does not count only those who left descendants. The line then continues through Jether's brother Jonathan.
32.notes: This Jether is unrelated to Jether the Ishmaelite, father of Amasa (2:17). This Jonathan is unrelated to Saul's son Jonathan.

33.brief: Jonathan’s sons are Peleth and Zaza, and the verse sums up that these were the sons of Jerahmeel. This closes the main listing of Jerahmeel’s family before the special account of Sheshan.
33.explain:
“The sons of Jonathan were Peleth and Zaza.”

The genealogy follows “Jonathan,” Jada's son, into the next generation. His sons were “Peleth” and “Zaza,” otherwise unknown.

“These were the sons of Jerahmeel.”

The verse sums up the main listing of Jerahmeel's family. “These were the sons of Jerahmeel” marks the end of this section before the special account of Sheshan's family in verses 34–41. The record of Hezron's firstborn has traced several branches, some continuing and some ending, all preserved by name.

34.brief: Sheshan had no sons, only daughters, and he had an Egyptian servant named Jarha. The record introduces a situation that left the continuation of his line in question.
34.explain:
“Now Sheshan had no sons, only daughters.”

The list returns to “Sheshan” (2:31) and explains a situation that threatened his family's continuation. He “had no sons, only daughters.” In Israel, family property and name normally passed through sons. A man with no sons faced the end of his line. The law made provision for daughters to inherit in such cases (Numbers 27:1–11), but the continuation of the family name was still a concern.

“And Sheshan had an Egyptian servant whose name was Jarha.”

Sheshan's household included “an Egyptian servant” named “Jarha.” The record preserves both his name and his background. The verse introduces the solution that the next verse describes.
34.notes:
The Hebrew word 'eved can mean servant or slave. The text does not describe Jarha's legal status, how he came to Sheshan's household, or whether he had embraced Israel's faith.

Numbers 36:6–8 required daughters who inherited, like Zelophehad’s, to marry “within the family of their father’s tribe.” Sheshan’s daughter instead married an Egyptian servant, so the arrangement may reflect a different custom for preserving a family line.

35.brief: Sheshan gives his daughter to Jarha his servant as wife, and she bears him Attai. Through Sheshan’s daughter and his Egyptian servant the family continues, and both have a place in Judah’s record.
35.explain:
“Sheshan gave his daughter to Jarha his servant as wife,”

Sheshan's solution was to give “his daughter” in marriage to “Jarha his servant.” By this marriage, Sheshan's line would continue through his daughter's children. The daughter is not named, but her place in the family is clear. Jarha, an Egyptian, became part of a family of Judah.

“and she bore him Attai.”

The daughter bore Jarha a son, “Attai.” Through Sheshan's daughter and his Egyptian servant the family continued, and both have a place in Judah's record. The family history of Judah cannot be reduced to an unbroken line of Israelite fathers and sons. God preserved this family through a daughter and a foreigner. The text records the arrangement without endorsing slavery or describing the details of Jarha's position after the marriage.
35.notes:
Documents from Nuzi in northern Mesopotamia record comparable arrangements. In one adoption contract a man named Nashwi adopts Wullu, gives him his daughter in marriage, and provides that if Nashwi has no son of his own, Wullu is to receive his household gods. Other Nuzi contracts record the adoption of a stranger, sometimes a slave, by a childless couple.

Sheshan’s arrangement may reflect a similar practice, in which Jarha’s children were counted as Sheshan’s descendants, though the text does not say that Jarha was adopted.

36.brief: Attai fathered Nathan, and Nathan fathered Zabad. The line descended from Sheshan’s daughter and Jarha is now traced forward generation by generation.
36.explain:
“Attai begot Nathan, and Nathan begot Zabad;”

The line descended from Sheshan's daughter and Jarha is now traced forward, generation by generation. “Attai” fathered “Nathan,” and Nathan fathered “Zabad.” The form of the list changes here to a simple chain of father and son, using “begot” for each step. This is one of the longest single lines in Judah's genealogy outside the royal line, stretching from Attai through thirteen generations to Elishama (2:41). A family that seemed about to end continued for many generations.
36.notes: This Nathan is unrelated to Nathan the prophet (1 Chronicles 17:1) and Nathan the son of David (1 Chronicles 3:5).

37.brief: Zabad fathered Ephlal, and Ephlal fathered Obed. This Obed is a descendant of Jerahmeel, distinct from Obed the grandfather of David in verse 12.
37.explain:
“Zabad begot Ephlal, and Ephlal begot Obed;”

The line continues from “Zabad” through “Ephlal” to “Obed.” This “Obed” is a descendant of Jerahmeel through Sheshan's daughter, distinct from Obed the grandfather of David (2:12). The repetition of familiar names within the same tribe shows how certain names were passed down among Judah's families. The genealogy keeps the generations in order, preserving the continuity of a line that had nearly ended.

38.brief: Obed fathered Jehu, and Jehu fathered Azariah, as the line descended from Sheshan’s daughter and Jarha continues.
38.explain:
“Obed begot Jehu, and Jehu begot Azariah;”

The line continues from “Obed” through “Jehu” to “Azariah.” This “Jehu” is a different man from Jehu the king of Israel (2 Kings 9–10) and from Jehu the prophet (2 Chronicles 19:2). This “Azariah” is one of many men by that name in Chronicles (compare 2:8). The line descended from Sheshan's daughter and Jarha continues without interruption.

39.brief: Azariah fathered Helez, and Helez fathered Eleasah.
39.explain:
“Azariah begot Helez, and Helez begot Eleasah;”

The line continues from “Azariah” through “Helez” to “Eleasah.” A man named Helez also appears among David's mighty men (1 Chronicles 11:27), though he is called a Pelonite, and there is no clear link to this family. Chronicles gives no details about these men. The steady chain of names is the point: generation followed generation in the family that God had preserved through an unexpected marriage.

40.brief: Eleasah fathered Sismai, and Sismai fathered Shallum.
40.explain:
“Eleasah begot Sismai, and Sismai begot Shallum;”

The line continues from “Eleasah” through “Sismai” to “Shallum.” Shallum was a common name, borne by a king of Israel (2 Kings 15:10–15), a son of Josiah (1 Chronicles 3:15), and others. This Shallum is a descendant of Sheshan through his daughter and Jarha. The genealogy nears the end of the line.

41.brief: Shallum fathered Jekamiah, and Jekamiah fathered Elishama, the last name in the line. A family that continued through a daughter and an Egyptian servant endured for many generations in Judah’s record.
41.explain:
“Shallum begot Jekamiah, and Jekamiah begot Elishama.”

The line ends with “Jekamiah” and his son “Elishama.” Elishama is the last name in the line descended from Sheshan's daughter and Jarha. From Attai to Elishama there are thirteen generations. A family that continued through a daughter and an Egyptian servant endured for many generations in Judah's record. Sheshan had no sons, but his name was not lost. The list shows a family preserved and remembered, through an arrangement that may have seemed unusual to many Israelites.
41.notes: The genealogy gives no ages or historical markers for this line, so the period its generations cover cannot be fixed.

42.brief: The record returns to Caleb, Jerahmeel’s brother, naming Mesha his firstborn, the father of Ziph, and the sons of Mareshah the father of Hebron. Here father of a town may describe a founding or leading ancestor of its people rather than a literal parent of a place.
42.explain:
“The descendants of Caleb the brother of Jerahmeel were”

The record returns to “Caleb,” Hezron's son and “the brother of Jerahmeel.” His earlier family was listed in verses 18–24. This second section (2:42–55) adds further descendants, many of them linked to towns in Judah.

“Mesha, his firstborn, who was the father of Ziph,”

“Mesha” was Caleb's firstborn. He is called “the father of Ziph.” Ziph was a town in the hill country of Judah, southeast of Hebron. The Wilderness of Ziph was where David hid from Saul (1 Samuel 23:14). “Father of” here likely describes a founding or leading ancestor of the town's people rather than a literal parent of a place.

“and the sons of Mareshah the father of Hebron.”

The second part of the verse names “Mareshah,” called “the father of Hebron.” Mareshah and Hebron were both towns in Judah. Hebron was one of the most important cities in Judah, where David first reigned as king (1 Chronicles 3:4; 11:1–3). Family and place are bound together in these lists.
42.notes:
The Hebrew of this verse is difficult. The phrase “and the sons of Mareshah” seems to introduce another son of Caleb, but its relationship to Mesha is unclear. The ancient Greek translation known as the Septuagint reads ‘Mareshah his firstborn.’ Translations handle the verse in various ways.

This Mesha is unrelated to Mesha the king of Moab (2 Kings 3:4).

43.brief: Hebron’s sons are Korah, Tappuah, Rekem, and Shema. Names that also belong to places show how family and settlement are bound together in these lists.
43.explain:
“The sons of Hebron were Korah, Tappuah, Rekem, and Shema.”

The genealogy follows “Hebron,” the son of Mareshah (2:42). His four sons are named. “Tappuah” is also the name of a town in Judah's lowland (Joshua 15:34), and “Shema” is the name of a town in the Negev (Joshua 15:26). Names that also belong to places show how family and settlement are bound together in these lists. A clan and the town it founded or occupied could share a name. “Korah” here is unrelated to Korah the son of Esau (1:35) or Korah the Levite (Numbers 16).

44.brief: Shema fathered Raham the father of Jorkoam, and Rekem fathered Shammai. The record follows two of Hebron’s sons into the next generation.
44.explain:
“Shema begot Raham the father of Jorkoam,”

Chronicles follows two of Hebron's sons. “Shema” fathered “Raham,” who is called “the father of Jorkoam.” Jorkoam was probably a town, perhaps the Jokdeam of Joshua 15:56.

“and Rekem begot Shammai.”

“Rekem” fathered “Shammai.” This Shammai is distinct from Shammai the son of Onam (2:28). The list follows these two branches of Hebron's family into the next generation, continuing to link persons and places.

45.brief: Shammai’s son was Maon, and Maon was the father of Beth Zur. The line ends with a town of Judah associated with this family.
45.explain:
“And the son of Shammai was Maon,”

Shammai's son was “Maon.” Maon was also a town in the hill country of Judah, south of Hebron. Nabal, whose wife Abigail later married David, lived in Maon and was “of the house of Caleb” (1 Samuel 25:2–3).

“and Maon was the father of Beth Zur.”

Maon is called “the father of Beth Zur,” another town of Judah, north of Hebron. Rehoboam later fortified Beth Zur (2 Chronicles 11:7), and in Nehemiah's time a district of Beth Zur sent workers to rebuild Jerusalem's wall (Nehemiah 3:16). The line ends with a town associated with Caleb's family, showing how a clan's history became the history of a place.

46.brief: Ephah, Caleb’s concubine, bore Haran, Moza, and Gazez, and Haran fathered a son also named Gazez. The children of a concubine are included within Caleb’s family record.
46.explain:
“Ephah, Caleb's concubine, bore Haran, Moza, and Gazez;”

The record names “Ephah, Caleb's concubine.” A concubine was a secondary wife whose children usually did not share fully in the inheritance (compare 1:32). Her children are still included within Caleb's family record. Her sons were “Haran, Moza,” and “Gazez.” “Moza” may be connected with the town of Mozah in Benjamin (Joshua 18:26).

“and Haran begot Gazez.”

Haran fathered a son also named “Gazez,” the same name as his brother. Naming a son after a relative was common. The genealogy includes the children of a concubine as members of Caleb's family.
46.notes: Ephah appears as a man's name in 1:33 (a son of Midian) and 2:47 (a son of Jahdai). Here it is a woman's name. Several Hebrew names were used for both men and women.

47.brief: The sons of Jahdai are listed: Regem, Jotham, Geshan, Pelet, Ephah, and Shaaph. Jahdai’s connection to the surrounding names is not explained, reflecting the compressed nature of these records.
47.explain:
“And the sons of Jahdai were Regem, Jotham, Geshan, Pelet, Ephah, and Shaaph.”

Chronicles names six sons of “Jahdai.” Jahdai's connection to the surrounding names is not explained. He may have been a son of Caleb, a son of Ephah the concubine, or the head of another clan associated with Caleb's family. The compressed nature of these records sometimes leaves relationships unstated. “Shaaph” appears again in verse 49 as a son of Maachah; the two may be different men. The list preserves what it received without filling in every gap.
47.notes: Some older interpreters suggested that Jahdai is another name for Moza (2:46) or that Jahdai was another concubine of Caleb. Neither suggestion has firm support in the text.

48.brief: Maachah, another concubine of Caleb, bore Sheber and Tirhanah. A second concubine’s children are also given their place.
48.explain:
“Maachah, Caleb's concubine, bore Sheber and Tirhanah.”

A second concubine of Caleb, “Maachah,” is named. Her sons were “Sheber” and “Tirhanah.” Like Ephah's children (2:46), Maachah's children are given their place in Caleb's family. The name Maachah was common and was borne by several women in Scripture, including one of David's wives, the mother of Absalom (1 Chronicles 3:2). The record honors the secondary branches of Caleb's family alongside the main lines.

49.brief: Maachah also bore Shaaph the father of Madmannah and Sheva the father of Machbenah and of Gibea, and Caleb’s daughter was Achsah. The name Achsah also appears as the daughter of Caleb the son of Jephunneh (Joshua 15:13–17), so the relationship of that notice to this Caleb family record requires care.
49.explain:
“She also bore Shaaph the father of Madmannah,”

Maachah also bore “Shaaph,” who is called “the father of Madmannah.” Madmannah was a town in the Negev of Judah (Joshua 15:31).

“Sheva the father of Machbenah and the father of Gibea.”

Another son, “Sheva,” was “the father of Machbenah and the father of Gibea.” These were probably towns in Judah. This “Gibea” is distinct from Gibeah of Benjamin, Saul's hometown.

“And the daughter of Caleb was Achsah.”

The verse ends by naming Caleb's daughter, “Achsah.” Elsewhere, Achsah is the daughter of Caleb the son of Jephunneh, who gave her in marriage to Othniel for capturing Kirjath Sepher (Joshua 15:16–17; Judges 1:12–13). Her appearance here in the family of Caleb the son of Hezron raises a question about how the two Calebs' families are related.
49.notes: Some interpreters think that Chronicles has combined material from the two Caleb clans, which may have been closely related; others think the Caleb of this verse is Caleb the son of Jephunneh; still others suggest two women of the same name, or take “daughter” in the broader sense of a later female descendant. The genealogy does not identify which is correct.

50.brief: A new heading introduces further descendants of Caleb, the sons of Hur, the firstborn of Ephrathah, beginning with Shobal the father of Kirjath Jearim. Hur’s family is linked with towns that would matter in Israel’s later history.
50.explain:
“These were the descendants of Caleb:”

A new heading introduces further descendants of Caleb. The phrase may conclude the preceding list (2:42–49) or introduce the following one (2:50–55); the NKJV takes it as introducing what follows.

“The sons of Hur, the firstborn of Ephrathah,”

The genealogy returns to “Hur,” Caleb's son by Ephrath (2:19), here called “the firstborn of Ephrathah.” Hur's descendants include Bezalel (2:20), and now the record lists more of his family.

“were Shobal the father of Kirjath Jearim,”

The first son of Hur named here is “Shobal,” called “the father of Kirjath Jearim.” Kirjath Jearim was a town on the border of Judah and Benjamin. It is remembered as the place where the ark of God remained after the Philistines returned it (1 Samuel 7:1–2), and from which David brought it up to Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 13:5–6). First Samuel 7:2 mentions twenty years before describing Israel's lament and Samuel's appeal. That period does not tell us how long the ark remained there before David moved it to Jerusalem. Hur's family is linked with towns that would matter in Israel's later history.
50.notes:
The Hebrew reads literally ‘These were the sons of Caleb son of Hur, the firstborn of Ephrathah.’ The KJV follows that wording (‘the sons of Caleb the son of Hur’). The NKJV, like the ancient Greek translation known as the Septuagint (‘Hor’s sons,’ using the Greek form of the name Hur) and modern translations such as the ESV, NIV, and NASB, reads ‘the sons of Hur,’ which agrees with 2:19, where Hur is Caleb’s son.

This Shobal, son of Hur, is unrelated to Shobal the son of Seir (1:38). A Shobal is also listed among Judah's sons in 4:1–2, probably the same man as here.

51.brief: Hur’s other sons are Salma the father of Bethlehem and Hareph the father of Beth Gader. Bethlehem, the town of David, is associated here with Caleb’s descendants through Hur.
51.explain:
“Salma the father of Bethlehem,”

The next son of Hur named here is “Salma,” called “the father of Bethlehem.” Bethlehem, the town of David's birth, is here associated with Caleb's descendants through Hur. Whether this Salma is the same as Salma the father of Boaz (2:11) is uncertain, but both are connected with Bethlehem.

“and Hareph the father of Beth Gader.”

The third son of Hur named here, “Hareph,” was “the father of Beth Gader,” perhaps the Geder of Joshua 12:13. Chronicles shows how families of Judah became identified with the towns they founded or settled. Bethlehem, a small town in Judah, would become famous as the birthplace of David and, centuries later, of Jesus (Micah 5:2; Matthew 2:1).
51.notes: The connection of Bethlehem with Caleb's descendants through Hur and Ephrathah helps explain the name “Bethlehem Ephrathah” (Micah 5:2) and the description of Jesse as “that Ephrathite of Bethlehem Judah” (1 Samuel 17:12).

52.brief: Shobal the father of Kirjath Jearim had descendants, including Haroeh and half of the families of Manuhoth. Shobal’s line is described both through persons and through groups of families.
52.explain:
“And Shobal the father of Kirjath Jearim had descendants:”

The list follows “Shobal” (2:50) into the next generation.

“Haroeh, and half of the families of Manuhoth.”

Shobal's descendants include “Haroeh” and “half of the families of Manuhoth.” Shobal's line is described both through persons and through groups of families. “Haroeh” may be the same as Reaiah, named as Shobal's son in 4:2. “Manuhoth” may be connected with the Manahethites (2:54), of whom the other half descended from Salma. The family of Hur divided into clans that settled in different places.
52.notes: The Hebrew form of “Haroeh,” ha-ro'eh, has the same spelling as the expression translated ‘the seer’ in 1 Samuel 9:9. In that verse, “seer” is an older term for a prophet.

53.brief: The families of Kirjath Jearim are named as the Ithrites, the Puthites, the Shumathites, and the Mishraites, and from them came the Zorathites and the Eshtaolites. The record traces how clans from one town gave rise to the people of other places.
53.explain:
“The families of Kirjath Jearim were the Ithrites, the Puthites, the Shumathites, and the Mishraites.”

The record names four clans of “Kirjath Jearim.” “The Ithrites” may be the clan of Ira and Gareb, two of David's mighty men (1 Chronicles 11:40). The others are otherwise unknown. These clans descended from Shobal, the father of Kirjath Jearim.

“From these came the Zorathites and the Eshtaolites.”

From these clans came the people of “Zorah” and “Eshtaol,” two towns in the lowland of Judah near the border with Dan. Samson was born near Zorah, and the Spirit of the LORD began to move upon him “between Zorah and Eshtaol” (Judges 13:25). The genealogy traces how clans from one town gave rise to the people of other places.
53.notes: Zorah and Eshtaol appear in both Judah's town list (Joshua 15:33) and Dan's allotment (Joshua 19:41). Those lists do not date a transfer of the towns from one tribe to the other. Chronicles records families connected with Kirjath Jearim as ancestors of the Zorathites and Eshtaolites; the precise history behind these overlapping associations is not supplied.

54.brief: The sons of Salma include Bethlehem, the Netophathites, Atroth Beth Joab, half of the Manahethites, and the Zorites. Here the language of sons includes towns and clans, showing that the genealogy records communities as well as individuals.
54.explain:
“The sons of Salma were Bethlehem, the Netophathites,”

Chronicles follows “Salma,” the father of Bethlehem (2:51). Here the language of sons includes towns and clans. “Bethlehem” is named as Salma's ‘son,’ meaning the town and its people. “The Netophathites” were the people of Netophah, a village near Bethlehem. Two of David's mighty men came from there (1 Chronicles 11:30), and Netophathites returned from exile with Zerubbabel (Nehemiah 7:26).

“Atroth Beth Joab, half of the Manahethites, and the Zorites.”

The list continues with “Atroth Beth Joab,” a place otherwise unknown, “half of the Manahethites,” of whom the other half descended from Shobal (2:52), and “the Zorites,” perhaps related to the Zorathites (2:53). The genealogy records communities as well as individuals, showing how families became settlements and settlements became part of Judah's identity.
54.notes: Levitical singers lived in “the villages of the Netophathites” after the exile (Nehemiah 12:28; compare 1 Chronicles 9:16).

55.brief: The chapter ends with the three families of scribes who dwelt at Jabez, the Tirathites, the Shimeathites, and the Suchathites, identified as Kenites who came from Hammath, the father of the house of Rechab. Judah’s record makes room for these scribal families and their associated peoples among its households.
55.explain:
“And the families of the scribes who dwelt at Jabez”

The chapter ends with “the families of the scribes” who lived at “Jabez,” a town apparently in Judah. “Scribes” were people skilled in writing, copying, and record-keeping. The location of Jabez is unknown. The name is also borne by the man whose prayer is recorded in 4:9–10, but the text does not connect them.

“were the Tirathites, the Shimeathites, and the Suchathites.”

Three scribal families are named. Their names are otherwise unknown.

“These were the Kenites who came from Hammath, the father of the house of Rechab.”

The scribal families are identified as “Kenites.” The Kenites were a non-Israelite people associated with Moses's father-in-law, who settled among the people of Judah (Judges 1:16). They came “from Hammath, the father of the house of Rechab.” The Rechabites were later known for their faithfulness to their ancestor's commands; Jeremiah held them up as an example of obedience (Jeremiah 35:1–19). Judah's record makes room for these scribal families and their associated peoples among its households. The chapter that began with the twelve sons of Israel ends with Kenite scribes, people of non-Israelite origin who were counted among Judah's families.
55.notes:
The meaning of the three family names is uncertain. The Latin Vulgate translates them as descriptions rather than names (‘singing and resounding and dwelling in tents’), and some later interpreters took the first to mean gatekeepers. Translations differ.

Jehonadab the son of Rechab supported Jehu against the worship of Baal (2 Kings 10:15–23), and his descendants refused to drink wine or build houses because of his command (Jeremiah 35:6–10). The relationship between Hammath, Rechab, and these scribal families is not explained further.
